text.what: A Polish-American bakery selling pączki — rich filled donuts, powidła or rose-petal jam inside, powdered or glazed — beside rye bread and coffee cake. One day a year it is the only thing anyone is there for.
text.story:
Pączki are medieval in Poland and were improved, Jędrzej Kitowicz wrote, by French cooks at the court of Augustus III until they came out lighter. The dough is richer than a jelly donut's — eggs, fat, sugar, yeast, sometimes milk — and carries a spoonful of rectified spirit, which evaporates in the fryer and keeps the oil out.

The pale belt around the middle is read as proof the oil was fresh. In Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit and Windsor the tradition sits with the Polish communities, and Fat Tuesday is Paczki Day.
text.how: Fresh oil, and the bakers say so. Fried in batches all night before the day, filled and sugared as they cool.
text.today: Hamtramck, Michigan, runs a Paczki Day the city closes streets for. Chicago bakeries post limits.

text.what: A small family grocery in the Mississippi or Arkansas Delta with a hot counter — and, in some of them, donuts fried in the morning beside the rest of the cooking.
text.story:
Chinese labourers were recruited to the Delta by cotton planters during Reconstruction, most of them men from the Siyi region of Guangdong. By the end of the 1870s they had left the plantations and opened small family groceries in Delta towns, and families followed in the early 1900s. The stores served Black customers that white-owned stores treated badly, in a state whose records classified the owners as "colored".

*Inference —* the donut counter in a Delta grocery belongs to the same logic as the egg rolls in a California donut shop: a family business open early with a fryer already lit adds the thing that sells at that hour. This project has not found a published history of Delta grocery donut counters, and says so rather than inventing one.
text.how: Cake batter, a small kettle, and a case by the register.
text.today: The Delta Chinese community has thinned as generations left for cities; the stores that remain are fewer and older.

text.what: Coffee first, donut second, at a counter that measures itself in how fast the line moves. The New England model, and the one the rest of the country meets as a drive-thru.
text.story:
Bill Rosenberg opened the Open Kettle in Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1948, selling donuts and coffee; in May 1950 he renamed it Dunkin' Donuts. He had been selling food to factories and construction sites and found donuts and coffee were what people bought. Franchising started in 1955. Johnny Spartos, running the original Quincy shop, talked Rosenberg into a donut with a handle, made for dunking.

The chain's growth came partly by absorption: in 1990 it took over Mister Donut — founded by Rosenberg's former partner Harry Winokur — and Dawn Donuts, converting the shops.

Density is the New England fact. The Providence metropolitan area has been cited as having the most donut shops per capita in the United States: 25.3 per 100,000 people, as of 13 January 2010.

text.what: A seasonal counter at a cider mill, orchard or farm stand, running one machine and one product: cake donuts with cider in the batter, sugared and handed over hot in a paper bag.
text.story:
Donuts belonged to autumn before anyone sold them at an orchard: the slaughter season produced the surplus fat you fried in. Cider donuts themselves go back at least to the late nineteenth century — a 1901 piece in The Buffalo Enquirer has them at Halloween parties.

What made them a roadside business was Adolph Levitt's 1921 machine, which fried rings of batter methodically and in public. Cider-selling farm stands took it up quickly. The Doughnut Corporation of America may have sold the first commercial cider donut, a "sweet cider doughnut", in 1951.

The season runs with the apples: September into November or December.
text.how: One depositor over one kettle, in view of the queue. Cider is reduced first, or the batter carries too much water. Donuts go into cinnamon sugar and then into a bag that goes translucent on the drive home.
text.today: Grocery stores start selling them in August and Dunkin' has run them as a seasonal item, which Food & Wine has pointed out is unlikely to involve fresh-pressed cider.

text.story:
The breakfast burrito is New Mexican before it is anything else. Tia Sophia's, a diner in Santa Fe, claims the first use of the term on a menu in 1975, though a tortilla rolled around eggs, bacon, potatoes and cheese was on New Mexican tables well before that. The fast-food chains followed — McDonald's in the late 1980s, Sonic, Hardee's and Carl's Jr. through the 1990s, Taco Bell in 2014.

The donut shop sits in the same slot as those chains: open early, one window, a driver in a truck. *Inference —* a counter already selling coffee at five in the morning has a griddle's worth of spare capacity and a customer who wants something salty, which is the same argument the California shops make about egg rolls.

names.said: A coffee regular and a bacon egg and cheese on a roll, and the donut is an afterthought until it isn't.

text.what: Donuts sold from a deli, bodega or coffee shop rather than a donut shop: a tray by the register, a grill behind the counter, and a bacon egg and cheese on a kaiser roll doing most of the business.
text.story:
A bodega is a small owner-operated store selling hot and prepared food, often open late, defined by the city's health department as a store that sells milk, meat or eggs, is not a specialty store, and has no more than two registers. New York had an estimated 13,000 of them in 2020, and they are tied in the public mind to immigrant and Puerto Rican New York.

The bacon, egg and cheese is culturally particular to the city, where it comes on a kaiser roll. The donut arrives alongside it as the sweet half of the same transaction.

Greek immigrants ran a large share of the city's coffee shops and diners, and the Anthora cup — blue and white, Greek meander, "We Are Happy To Serve You" — was designed for exactly this trade.
text.how: Donuts are bought in, not fried on site, in most of these counters. The kitchen is a grill, not a kettle.
text.today: Dedicated donut shops in the city are a different business with different prices. The corner counter still moves more of them.

The fasnacht is a pantry-clearing food: lard, sugar, fat and butter used up before Lent. Lancaster, York, Lebanon and Berks counties keep it, and the day is known locally as Fastnacht Day rather than Shrove Tuesday. Parts of Maryland call them kinklings or kuechles, and bakeries there sell them only on that Tuesday.

Polish-American communities in the United States have largely moved pączki from the Thursday before to this same Tuesday, so in a city with both populations, one Tuesday carries two traditions and two arguments about which dough is better.

names.name: The Southern California pink box
names.said: Nobody calls it a style. You say "the donut shop", and everyone knows which corner of which strip mall you mean.

text.what: An independent counter, usually in a strip mall, usually open before five in the morning, frying both doughs in one small kitchen and selling them out of a matte pink box. Glazed raised, cake rings, buttermilk bars, fritters, bear claws, maple bars, holes in a bag. Coffee in a paper cup. Often, on the same board: egg rolls, croissant sandwiches, chow mein, boba, or a breakfast burrito.
text.story:
Ted Ngoy left Cambodia with his wife and three children in 1975, ahead of the Khmer Rouge, and came through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program to Camp Pendleton. He took a janitor's job at a Lutheran church in Tustin and a second job at a gas station, noticed how busy a local donut shop was, and asked to learn the trade. An affirmative-action hiring program at the Winchell's chain trained him; he managed a store in Newport Beach and put his wife and nephew to work in it. In 1977 he bought his own shop, Christy's Donuts in La Habra, and named every shop he bought afterwards the same thing.

By 1979 he had more than 25 shops. He grew tired of running them himself, so he trained relatives and refugees and leased shops to them — "I sponsored more than 100 families", he said, and claimed each on official paperwork as kin. By 1987 he had 32 Christy's; at the peak he reckoned 65. The leasing model is the part that mattered: a family arrived, learned a trade in a month, took a shop, and a few years later sold or leased a shop to the next family.

KQED reported in 2021 that roughly 90 percent of California's 5,000-plus independent donut shops were Cambodian-owned. The pink box itself is attributed to Ngoy and Ning Yen, who were helping other Cambodians set up shops: cheaper matte pink stock instead of the glossy white box.

Why the second menu is there is not a mystery either. Jolly Chan, who opened China Express and Donut by the 24th Street BART station in San Francisco in 1993, put it plainly to KQED: "We have to sell more stuff to make up the rent and the expense."
text.how: One fryer, two doughs. Raised dough goes up overnight and is cut, proofed and fried first; cake batter is dropped from a depositor after. Glaze table by the door. Everything is done before the first commuter, and the case is not restocked — when the bars are gone they are gone. A second warmer holds whatever the shop also sells hot.
text.today: The model is under pressure from rents, from flour and shortening prices, and from the second generation going to college rather than to the bench at two in the morning. Shops still open, close and change hands quietly; the pink box outlives the owner's name on the sign. *Inference —* the box is the most portable piece of the whole thing, which is why it turns up in cities that never had the shops.

names.said: The sign goes on and cars turn in. That is the whole marketing plan and it has worked since 1937.

text.what: A glazed raised ring handed over hot, minutes out of the fryer, with the glaze still moving. Built around a window you can watch the line through, and a lit sign that says the fryer is running.
text.story:
Vernon Rudolph bought a yeast-raised recipe from a New Orleans chef, rented a building at 534 South Main Street in Winston-Salem in 1937 — now historic Old Salem — and sold to grocery stores. He also sold hot donuts to people who turned up during production, which ran from midnight to four in the morning. That is the origin of the whole idea: the hot donut was a by-product of the wholesale schedule, sold to whoever was awake.

The recipe traces back further, to Rudolph's uncle Ishmael Armstrong's general store in Paducah, Kentucky, and — by one account — to an Ohio River barge cook named Joseph LeBeouf, whose light doughnuts contained potatoes. The first store outside the South opened in Akron, Ohio, in 1939. A local architect, Benny Dinkins, drew the logo.

In the early 2010s the company began building shops with tunnel ovens so the hot sign could stay on all day, which is a different proposition from a sign that tells you the night shift is still going.

names.name: The Texas kolache counter
names.said: Order a kolache in Texas and you will probably get sausage in it, which a Czech Texan will tell you is a klobasnek.

text.what: A donut counter that also sells kolaches — and, in Texas, mostly klobasniky: sausage, ham, egg, cheese or jalapeño wrapped in sweet kolache dough. Sold from gas stations, strip-mall shops and dedicated kolache bakeries across the state, well outside the Czech settlement belt.
text.story:
Two different pastries carry one name here. A traditional kolache came with Moravian immigrants: sweet dough with a fruit or cheese filling in a well on top. The klobasnek was invented by Czechs who had already settled in Texas — sausage wrapped in that same dough. Texans not of Czech descent call both kolaches; Texans of Czech descent call the savoury ones klobasniky and mean it.

The town of West, in McLennan County, has one of the largest concentrations of Czech Texans in the state and was designated "Home of the Official Kolache of the Texas Legislature" in 1997. Westfest keeps the day.

The donut shop picked it up because it sells at the same hour to the same driver. Fillings widened from klobása to hot dogs, ham and egg, cheese and peppers, and in some shops boudin, the Cajun pork-and-rice sausage.
text.how: Kolache dough is enriched and proofed like a sweet roll, wrapped around the sausage and baked, not fried — which means a Texas donut shop is running an oven as well as a kettle.
text.today: Kolaches travel where Texans travel. The word now shows up on donut counters in Oklahoma, Louisiana and Colorado, usually meaning the sausage kind.

text.what: A sweet yeast dough — bread dough carrying more shortening than usual — filled with almond paste and sometimes raisins, shaped in a semicircle with slices cut along the curved edge so the sections separate as it proofs, into toes.
text.story:
The name is first attested on 13 March 1914, in a newspaper advertisement for the Geibel German Bakery in Sacramento, California. By the next year bear claws were on the breakfast menu at Hamburger's in Los Angeles, then the largest department store west of Chicago. The Sacramento Bee reports no earlier public reference; a Sacramento historian cautioned against crowning the city as the origin on that evidence alone.

text.what: A ring of thick batter, not dough, raised by baking powder or soda rather than yeast and dropped straight into the fat from a depositor. It is denser, shorter and smaller than a raised ring — cake rings run 24 to 28 grams against the raised ring's 38 — and it takes sugar, cinnamon sugar or a heavy icing better than it takes a thin glaze.
text.story:
The cake ring appears in American cookbooks in the 1830s, after pearlash — a potash refined for baking — became easy to buy, and it is the ring that industrialised. Yeast wants hours and a warm room; chemical leavening wants a mixer and a clock. When doughnut shops were streamlining production in the 1920s and 1930s, most bakers went the cake route because baking soda behaved the same way every morning and machines could be built around it.

The structural difference is in the flour as much as the lift: cake rings use cake flour, around 7 to 8 percent protein, which is why they crumb rather than pull.

The fat numbers depend on who you ask, and the two accounts do not agree. One puts cake at about 20 percent oil against yeast's 25; another puts cake at 20 to 25 percent and yeast at 25 to 35. Neither names a laboratory. What both agree on is the direction: the raised ring spends longer in the fat and comes out carrying more of it, and the cake ring makes up the difference with shortening mixed in before it ever gets there.
text.how: Beat a soft batter — cake flour, sugar, eggs, shortening, milk, baking powder. Rest it. Drop rings into 190 to 198 °C fat through a depositor, or cut them from a soft rolled dough. Fry roughly 90 seconds, turning once; one account has commercial cake rings out in 30 to 45 seconds at 191 °C. Sugar or ice them after they cool a little, because a hot cake ring drinks a thin glaze and goes soggy.
text.today: Cake is the dough that holds a flavour — buttermilk, sour cream, blueberry, chocolate, cider — so a shop that runs both doughs usually runs its specials on this side of the case.

names.name: Cider donut
names.said: Bought hot at the mill, in a paper bag that goes translucent on the drive home.

text.what: An American cake donut flavoured with apple cider, cinnamon and nutmeg in the batter, usually rolled in cinnamon or granulated sugar. Denser and moister than a plain cake ring because the cider is in the batter, not on it.
text.story:
Cider donuts go back at least to the late nineteenth century — a 1901 piece in The Buffalo Enquirer has them at Halloween parties. Donuts had long belonged to autumn anyway: the slaughter season produced the surplus fat you fried them in.

The modern version follows the machine. Adolph Levitt's 1921 doughnut machine let anyone fry circles of batter methodically, and cider-selling farm stands took it up fast. The first commercially produced cider donut may have been the Doughnut Corporation of America's "sweet cider doughnut" in 1951.

Season runs with the apples: September through November or December. Grocery stores put them out as early as August, and Food & Wine has noted that a year-round cider donut is unlikely to have fresh-pressed cider in it.
text.how: Reduce cider, beat it into a cake batter with cinnamon and nutmeg, drop rings, fry, and roll in sugar while hot.
text.today: Sold at orchards, cider mills and farm stands as part of a day out, and by the half-dozen at the register of every farm store in the Northeast in October.

names.name: Fastnacht
names.said: Spelled six ways in six counties, and everybody thinks theirs is the spelling.

text.what: A Pennsylvania Dutch fried donut, often made with potato dough, eaten in the days of Carnival and above all on Shrove Tuesday. Square or diamond cut, sometimes with a slit rather than a hole, sometimes plain, sometimes dusted with table sugar.
text.story:
The point of it is the pantry. Fasnachts were made to use up lard, sugar, fat and butter before Lent, when households gave them up. The Pennsylvania Dutch counties — Lancaster, York, Lebanon, Berks and around — keep the day, and in eastern Pennsylvania the supermarkets carry them. Parts of Maryland call them kinklings or kuechles and bakeries sell them on Shrove Tuesday only.

The Polish pączek is the same idea a few hundred miles west. In Poland pączki are eaten on the Thursday before; in Polish-American communities the date has moved to Fasnacht Day, which is to say Tuesday.
text.how: Potato dough, risen, rolled, cut in squares or diamonds, slit in the middle, fried. Eaten with butter or golden syrup, which is the part outsiders find strange and Pennsylvania finds obvious.
text.today: Churches and fire halls still sell them by pre-order, by the dozen, and stop when the batch is gone.

names.name: French cruller
names.said: The light one. Ridged, hollow, gone in three bites.

text.what: A ring extruded from choux paste — flour cooked into butter and water, then beaten with eggs — piped through a star tip so it fries up ridged and hollow, and glazed thin. No yeast, no baking powder: steam lifts it.
text.story:
Cruller is Dutch, from kruller, from krullen, to curl, and it arrives in America in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries with Pennsylvania Dutch settlers. In Europe the shape is a twist or a plaited rectangle pulled through itself; in North America the word covers both a small loaf- or stick-shaped cake doughnut and the French cruller, the choux ring. Milwaukee's cruller is the loaf kind: a glazed cake bar with a crunchy shell.

The word travels further than the pastry. Youtiao, the Chinese fried stick, gets called a Chinese cruller in English; so does mahua, the twisted one.
text.how: Cook the paste, beat in the eggs, pipe rings onto squares of paper, and slide them paper and all into the fat so they keep their shape. The paper lifts off once they set. Glaze while warm.
text.today: Few independent shops make them, because the paste is a different process from everything else on the bench, and the ones that do say so on the sign.

names.name: Glazed raised
names.said: Ask for a glazed and nobody asks which kind. It means this one.

text.what: A ring of yeast dough, proofed until it is full of gas, fried about two and a half minutes, then dragged through a thin sugar glaze while it is still hot enough to melt it. The glaze sets into a shell you can hear. Yeast-raised rings run larger and taller than cake rings and average around 38 grams apiece.
text.story:
The raised ring is the older idea and the harder one to run. Dutch settlers brought olykoek — oil cake — to New Amsterdam in the early eighteenth century, balls of sweetened dough fried in hog fat; Washington Irving put them in print in 1809 as "dough-nuts, or oly koeks". The hole arrives in the middle of the nineteenth century, credited by long habit to Hanson Gregory, a New England sailor who said he punched one out with a tin pepper box in 1847 at sixteen because the middles came out raw.

*Tradition holds —* that the hole was about heat reaching the centre. Culinary historian Linda Civitello writes that the hole made doughnuts cook faster; food writer Michael Krondl reckons the ring shape came off recipes that called for a jumble, a ring-shaped cookie already on the table. By 1870 a cutter with two concentric circles was on sale and the argument stopped mattering to anyone but historians.

When shops automated in the 1920s the raised dough lost ground: it needs time to rise and it is harder to handle, so machinery and baking soda pushed bakers toward cake. The raised ring survived because it is the one people mean.
text.how: Mix a lean, sweet dough with baker's yeast. Let it rise, sheet it, cut rings, then proof the cut rings again in a warm box until they are light enough to float. Fry about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C, turning once. Glaze hot: a thin syrup of powdered sugar and water or milk goes on within a minute of the fryer, so it soaks the crust and sets clear.
text.today: Every shop in the country sells it and most sell nothing else in that volume. A raised ring goes stale faster than a cake ring, which is why a shop that opened at four in the morning tells you so, and why the tray at noon is not the tray at six.

names.name: Malasada
names.said: No hole, no filling unless you ask, and sugar all over your shirt.

text.what: A flattened round of yeasted dough, fried and rolled in sugar — cinnamon sugar, often — with no hole and traditionally no filling. Portuguese from Madeira; Hawaiian by adoption, and the islands sell more of them than anywhere on the mainland.
text.story:
The name is Portuguese: mal and assado, badly roasted, for the unstructured shape — or, another account has it, for the underdone dough inside. Malasadas descend from the mainland and Madeiran filhós, a product of the sixteenth-century sugar industry, and travelled through Macaronesia to the Azores, the Canaries and as far as Brazil. They are first described in the Dicionário Houaiss da Língua Portuguesa in 1609 and appear in the ledgers of the Convento da Encarnação in Lisbon between 1688 and 1762.

Portuguese contract labourers carried them to Hawaii, where they are called Hawaiian donuts often enough that the name has stuck to them in the rest of the country too. The Azorean malasada is a Carnival food; the Penedono filhós, made with brandy and olive oil instead of milk, is eaten year round, and the Portuguese agriculture directorate treats the two as distinct.
text.how: A rich yeast dough, rested, pulled into rounds by hand rather than cut, fried until it puffs, then dropped straight into a pan of granulated sugar.
text.today: Hawaii keeps a day for them. Shops sell them plain and filled — haupia, custard, guava — and the plain one is still the one that goes fastest.

names.name: Mochi donut
names.said: Eight balls in a ring, and you pull it apart rather than bite it.

text.what: A chewy donut made with glutinous rice flour or tapioca flour, usually formed as a ring of eight connected balls that pull apart. Moist, springy, and heavier in the hand than it looks.
text.story:
An early version traces to Hawaii in 1992, when Charmaine Ocasek made poi mochi — deep-fried balls of mashed taro and mochiko, Japanese sweet rice flour. In 2003 the Japanese chain Mister Donut launched pon de ring, named for the Brazilian cheese bread pão de queijo, and that eight-ball shape is the one that travelled: Japan, then Hawaii, then the mainland. Hawaii tends to pick up Japanese food before the rest of the country does.

Epicurious has pointed out the tangle in the name: neither pon de ring nor pão de queijo is typically made with glutinous rice flour — both lean on tapioca.
text.how: Rice or tapioca flour batter, piped as eight touching balls onto paper, fried, then iced in bright flavours.
text.today: Mochi donut counters opened across American cities through the 2020s, some as chains, some as a second case inside an older donut shop.

names.name: Old-fashioned
names.said: The one that looks broken on purpose.

text.what: A cake ring with a cracked surface and tapered edges, glazed or sugared so the glaze pools in the cracks. The crack is the point: more surface, crisper edge, and a ring that holds up to coffee longer than a raised one.
text.story:
The name has moved. Nineteenth-century cookbooks print old-fashioned doughnuts made with yeast; the old-fashioned in a shop case today is a cake ring raised with baking powder or soda, and has been described as a subset of the cake doughnut. Older counters called cake rings fry cakes, and the terms doughnut, cruller and fry cake have been argued over for as long as anyone has written them down.

Commercial versions often start from a dry batter mix that takes only water, which is one reason the same crack shows up in shops two thousand miles apart.
text.how: A stiff cake batter, chilled, cut thick. Into the fat cooler than a plain cake ring so the outside sets before the inside finishes lifting, which is what splits the surface. Glaze while warm.
text.today: Sour cream and buttermilk versions sell as their own items in most shops, and the plain glazed old-fashioned is the one that gets ordered with black coffee.

names.name: Pączki

text.what: A Polish filled donut: a flattened ball of rich dough — eggs, fat, sugar, yeast, sometimes milk — deep fried, filled with jam or cream, and finished in powdered sugar, icing, glaze or dried orange zest.
text.story:
Pączki have been known in Poland since at least the Middle Ages. Jędrzej Kitowicz wrote that under Augustus III, French cooks in Poland improved the dough until pączki came out lighter and springier.

Two details separate them from a jelly donut. A small amount of grain alcohol — traditionally rectified spirit — goes into the dough; as it evaporates it keeps the oil from soaking in. And the bright pale stripe around the middle, from floating in fresh fat, is read as evidence the oil had not been used and reused.

Traditional fillings are powidła, stewed plum jam, and wild rose petal jam. American shops fill them with everything else as well.

names.name: Spudnut
names.said: A word somebody trademarked, and the shops that still use it earned it.

text.what: A donut made with potato flour or mashed potato in the dough. Softer crumb, longer shelf life, and a faint savoury note under the sugar.
text.story:
Al and Bob Pelton of Salt Lake City ate potato doughnuts in Germany, then worked through wheat dough flavoured with potato water and mashed potato before landing on a dry potato mix that could be shipped — which is what made a franchise possible. They coined the word spudnut and opened in 1940.

The chain moved fast. Franchising began in 1946; in 1948 a new franchisee paid fifty dollars plus the cost of a hundred sacks of spudnut flour; by mid-1949 there were more than 225 shops in 31 states, more than 300 in 38 states by 1954, and 315 by 1968. The advertising ran "Coast to coast… Alaska to Mexico", with a cartoon Mr. Spudnut in parades.

The parent company is gone. Independent shops still trading under the name are the survivors of that system, not a chain.

text.what: A cylindrical deep-fried roll in a thick wheat skin — shredded cabbage, chopped meat, sometimes shrimp — eaten with the fingers out of a cellophane packet of duck sauce. Despite the name it generally has no egg in it, though egg white sometimes seals the seam.
text.story:
The egg roll is American. It is distinct from mainland Chinese spring rolls and first appears in the United States in the early twentieth century. Andrew Coe, who wrote Chop Suey: A Cultural History of Chinese Food in the United States, reckons the modern American egg roll was probably invented at a New York Chinese restaurant in the early 1930s by one of two chefs who each later claimed it: Lung Fong of Lung Fong's, or Henry Low of Port Arthur. Low's recipe, printed in the 1938 cookbook Cook at Home in Chinese, called for bamboo shoots, roast pork, shrimp, scallions, water chestnuts, salt, MSG, sugar, palm oil and pepper.

Why it is in a donut shop is a separate question with a plain answer: rent. Jolly Chan, who runs China Express and Donut in San Francisco, told KQED the combination "came out of necessity" — "we have to sell more stuff to make up the rent and the expense."

text.what: The fat itself: lard, beef tallow, vegetable shortening, or liquid oils — canola, soybean, palm.
text.story:
Shortening means any fat solid at room temperature; the word is about what it does to gluten, keeping strands short so pastry crumbs instead of stretching. Lard was the original. Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès invented margarine from beef tallow in 1869 and the industry moved to hydrogenated vegetable fats after.

Then it moved back. In 2015 the FDA found that artificial trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils were not generally recognised as safe; they were banned from foods sold in the United States from 18 June 2018, with limited extensions to 2020 and 2021. Crisco had already been reformulated in January 2007 to meet the zero-grams-per-serving definition. Denmark had capped industrial trans fats in 2004.

For a donut shop that meant a new fat, a different mouthfeel and, in many kitchens, a new supplier — inside a few years, and not by choice.
text.how: Filter it, top it up, and change it on a schedule the shop keeps in its head.

text.what: A shallow pan of thin sugar glaze beside the fryer, where raised rings are dragged through face-down within a minute of coming out of the fat.
text.story:
Glaze is a thin coating applied to food — here, powdered sugar with water or milk and sometimes a little fat, thin enough to run off and set clear. On a hot ring it soaks the crust and hardens into a shell; on a cool one it sits on top and stays tacky.

Cake rings are finished differently for the same reason: a hot cake ring drinks a thin glaze and goes soggy, so it takes sugar, cinnamon sugar or a heavier icing instead.
text.how: Dip, turn, lift, drain on a screen. The pan is topped up all morning and the glaze thickens as the shop warms.
text.today: The glaze table is where a shop's whole tray of raised donuts is either made or ruined, in about a minute each.

text.story:

A raised dough sets the clock. It has to be mixed, risen, cut, proofed and fried before opening, and none of those steps can be hurried by much.

text.what: A shallow open kettle of hot fat with a screen, where every donut in the shop is cooked, turned once, and lifted out.
text.story:
The two doughs want different heat. Yeast-raised rings fry about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C and absorb more fat for it — around 25 percent by weight. Cake rings fry about 90 seconds at 190 to 198 °C, turning once, and run near 20 percent, with extra shortening already in the batter.

The numbers are not settled. Another account puts cake at 20 to 25 percent and yeast at 25 to 35, and commercial cake rings at 30 to 45 seconds at 191 °C. Neither cites a laboratory, and this project reports both rather than picking.

text.today: Every other decision in the shop is downstream of how many rings fit on the surface of the fat at once.

text.what: Baker's yeast fermenting a sweet dough until it is full of gas — once in bulk, once again after the rings are cut.
text.story:
Proofing is the rest in which yeast ferments the dough and makes the gas that lifts it. Blooming is a different thing with the same word: suspending dry yeast in warm water to hydrate it, and to see whether it is still alive.

The raise is why the raised donut lost ground when shops automated in the 1920s. Yeast needs time and a warm room, and the dough is harder to handle; baking soda was predictable and easy to build a machine around, so most bakers went to cake.

text.what: A shop on Route 2 in North Kingstown, Rhode Island, cutting its donuts by hand since 1968, and the state's landmark of the trade.
text.story:
Frederick Alvin "Allie" Briggs opened Allie's Hand-Cut Do-nut Shop on 1 June 1968 in a former sub sandwich shop, with about forty dollars in hand and a seven-thousand-dollar debt. He was a dairy farmer from Point Judith with ten years of donut experience from a shop in Wakefield. He took $38 on the first day, selling close to a hundred dozen at 39 cents each.

In 1969 his son Ricky was killed by a drunk driver while out delivering donuts for the business alongside his cousin. Briggs nearly closed.
text.today: Customers drive in from Connecticut and Massachusetts. Saveur listed it among the country's best donut shops in 2008; Thrillist did the same in 2016.

text.what: The La Habra shop Ted Ngoy bought in 1977, and the name he put on every shop he bought after it.
text.story:
Christy's had not done well under its previous owners. It did well under the Ngoys, and they kept the name uniform across the shops they added — by 1979 more than 25 of them, by 1987 thirty-two, and at the peak Ngoy reckoned sixty-five. Ngoy and his wife took the American names Ted and Christy when they became citizens in 1985.

The shops were leased out to relatives and to refugee families Ngoy sponsored, which is how one shop turned into a trade for a community.
text.today: Shops trading as Christy's Donuts still exist in Southern California. This project has not verified which, if any, descend from the Ngoy shops, and does not claim it.

text.what: A drive-in donut counter on West Manchester Boulevard in Inglewood, under a 1950s rooftop donut big enough to be a landmark from the 405. Open around the clock.
text.story:
Russell Wendell, a donut machine salesman, founded a chain of drive-in shops called Big Donut in the late 1940s; the first opened in Westmont in 1951 and the second — this building — in 1952. Wendell moved on to his Pup 'N' Taco chain and sold the Inglewood shop in 1976 to Robert Eskow, who renamed it after his son Randy. Eskow sold it in 1978 to Ron and Larry Weintraub, who kept the name. It changed hands again in 2015.

Four of Wendell's big donuts survive; a fifth became a bagel. At their height there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins carrying 22-foot donuts, and the opening of the first one in December 1949 had clowns, jugglers, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging through the hole.
text.today: The rooftop donut gets photographed more than anything else in the trade, and the shop now runs additional locations under the same name.

text.story:
Kong Eap, who came to the United States in the 1970s, opened the bakery in 1985 — one of many Cambodian-American bakeries that opened in the area after Ted Ngoy's shops showed the way. text.what: A drive-through bakery in La Puente shaped like two giant donuts: you drive in through one hole, order, and drive out through the other.
text.story:
The first Donut Hole opened in 1963 in La Puente, though sources disagree — one says the La Puente shop was the second, opened in 1968, and dates the building anywhere from 1947 to 1962. What is settled is that the chain went out of business in 1979, the Lopez family bought the La Puente shop that year and held it until 2003, the Covina branch was remodelled beyond recognition and the rest were demolished. This one is the last working example.

Newlyweds drive through it. Some say for luck; others are less coy about the symbolism. Cars have hit the building more than once.
text.today: An example of programmatic architecture — a building shaped like what it sells — and among the most photographed donut shops in the country.

text.what: The New England sailor who said he punched the first hole in a donut in 1847, at sixteen, aboard a lime-trading ship.
text.story:
Gregory said he disliked how greasy twisted donuts were and how raw their centres came out, and punched a hole through the middle with the ship's tin pepper box, later teaching his mother the trick. text.what: The Cambodian refugee who turned one La Habra donut shop into a trade for a community, and lost the fortune it made him.
text.story:
Born in 1941 in Sisophon, near the Thai border, to a Chinese immigrant family; his mother, from Shantou, did not speak Khmer. He was sent to Phnom Penh to study in 1967, married Suganthini Khoeun, worked as a travel agent and tour guide, joined the military in 1970 and, through his brother-in-law Sak Sutsakhan, became a major and military attaché in Thailand. In 1975 he fled the Khmer Rouge with his wife and three children and reached Camp Pendleton through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

He took a janitor's job at Peace Lutheran Church in Tustin and a second job at a gas station, noticed a busy donut shop, and asked how it worked. An affirmative-action hiring programme at Winchell's trained him; he managed a store in Newport Beach. In 1977 he bought Christy's Donuts in La Habra.

By 1979 he had more than 25 shops. He began training relatives and refugees and leasing shops to them — "I sponsored more than 100 families" — living out of a motor home to open new ones. By 1987 there were 32 Christy's; at the peak he reckoned 65. He and his wife took citizenship in 1985 as Ted and Christy, bought a house at Lake Mission Viejo and a second at Big Bear, joined the Republican Party and held fundraisers for George H. W. Bush.

Then the gambling. A 1977 Las Vegas trip introduced him to blackjack; he returned monthly, forged his wife's signature on cheques, borrowed from relatives who leased shops from him and signed shops over when he could not repay. Gamblers Anonymous did not hold: "I cry, everybody cry. After cry, go back gambling."
text.today: Alice Gu's documentary The Donut King (2020) put the story in front of a national audience. The shops the model produced outlasted the fortune by decades.

text.story:
Rudolph (1915–1973) started at eighteen in his uncle Ishmael Armstrong's general store in Paducah, Kentucky, which sold popular doughnuts; the recipe is believed to trace to an Ohio River barge cook named Joseph LeBeouf, whose light doughnuts contained potatoes. Uncle and nephew moved to Nashville in 1934 and opened The Krispy Kreme Doughnut Company on Gallatin Road.

In 1937 Rudolph opened his own store, choosing Winston-Salem because Camel Cigarettes was headquartered there. He rented 534 South Main Street, in what is now historic Old Salem, sold to grocery stores, and sold hot donuts to people who came by during production between midnight and four in the morning. A local architect, Benny Dinkins, drew the logo. The first store outside the South opened in Akron, Ohio, in 1939.

text.what: The World War I canteens where Salvation Army volunteers fried donuts for American soldiers in France — and the reason there is a National Donut Day.
text.story:
After the United States entered the war in 1917 the Salvation Army sent a fact-finding mission to France, which concluded that enlisted men's needs could be met by canteens — "huts" — serving baked goods and providing writing supplies, stamps and mending. About 250 volunteers went. Baking was hard in abandoned buildings near the front, so two volunteers, Ensign Margaret Sheldon and Adjutant Helen Purviance, turned to donuts. They were an instant hit. Sheldon wrote of one day: "Today I made 22 pies, 300 donuts, 700 cups of coffee."

The women became known to the servicemen as Donut Girls. A misconception ties the donuts to the word doughboy; the term was in use decades earlier.
text.today: National Donut Day, first Friday in June, began in 1938 as a Chicago Salvation Army fundraiser honouring them.

text.what: In North America: either a small loaf- or stick-shaped cake donut, or the choux ring sold as a French cruller.
text.story:
From the Dutch kruller, from krullen, to curl. Pennsylvania Dutch settlers brought it in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. In Europe the shape is a twist or a plaited rectangle pulled through itself; northern Germany calls those Hirschhörner, deer horns, and Scandinavia makes them at Christmas — klejner in Danish, klenäter in Swedish.

Milwaukee's cruller is a glazed loaf-shaped cake donut with a crunchy shell. The Aberdeen crulla is Scottish, first attested in Edinburgh in 1829 and thought to copy the American cruller. Youtiao and mahua both get called Chinese crullers in English.

text.what: Two spellings of the same word. Doughnut is the older form and still dominates in print; donut is American, shorter, and on more signs.
text.story:
The first known printed use of donut is in George W. Peck's Peck's Bad Boy and his Pa, 1900: a character drinks a cup of coffee and eats a donut. John T. Edge writes that the short spelling was invented in the 1920s by the New York-based Display Doughnut Machine Corporation, which cut the word to make it easier for the foreign buyers it hoped would buy its machines. A Los Angeles Times piece of 10 August 1929 has Bailey Millard complaining he cannot swallow "the 'wel-dun donut'".

The two ran side by side for decades: The New York Times used both across a series of "National Donut Week" articles covering the 1939 World's Fair. Dunkin' — Open Kettle in 1948, renamed in 1950 — is the oldest surviving company using the short form. Krispy Kreme, per Oxford, is the notable exception that keeps the long one.

Hanson Gregory, an American sailor, claimed he invented the ring in 1847 aboard a lime-trading ship at sixteen, punching the middle out with the ship's tin pepper box because he disliked greasy dough and raw centres, and teaching his mother the trick. The Smithsonian has his mother, Elizabeth Gregory, making a deep-fried dough that used his spice cargo — nutmeg, cinnamon, lemon rind.

Other readings compete. Michael Krondl suggests the ring came off recipes calling for a jumble, a ring-shaped cookie already in use. Linda Civitello writes the hole was invented because it let the donut cook faster. By 1870 a two-circle cutter was in production and the question became academic.

text.what: A shop owned and worked by the family that runs it, as against a franchise or a company-owned store.
text.story:
The line is blurrier than the phrase suggests. A shop can buy its mix from a national flour company, carry a franchised name on the window, and still be owned outright by the family inside it — every Daylight Donuts store is independently owned and operated, and there are roughly 950 of them. A Spudnut sign may outlive the franchise that sold it. And a single family may hold three shops and run them all itself.

This project counts a shop as independent when no company owns it; the sign on the window is not the test.

text.what: The Dutch fried dough ball that came to New Amsterdam, and the American donut's direct ancestor: sweetened dough fried in fat, with no hole.
text.story:
Dutch settlers brought olykoek — oil cake — to New York in the early eighteenth century. Washington Irving put it in print in his 1809 History of New York: "an enormous dish of balls of sweetened dough, fried in hog's fat, and called dough-nuts, or oly koeks: a delicious kind of cake, at present scarce known in this city, excepting in genuine Dutch families."

The centres of those balls were the problem the ring solved. Elizabeth Gregory, by the Smithsonian's account, put hazelnuts or walnuts in the middle where the dough might not cook through — which is one reading of where the nut in doughnut comes from.

text.what: Oversize donuts built on or around Southern California shops to catch drivers: roadside novelty architecture, most of it from the decade after the Second World War.
text.story:
Randy's, beside the 405 near LAX, is the best known of four surviving big donuts built by Russell C. Wendell, who started the Big Do-Nut Drive-In chain in the 1940s. A fifth was converted into a bagel. At one point there were ten Do-Nut Drive-Ins with 22-foot rings — or thirty feet high, depending on the account. The first opened in December 1949 with clowns, jugglers, magicians, free coffee and a trapeze artist swinging from the middle of the hole.

Mrs. Chapman's Angel Food Donuts ran about twenty stores with slightly smaller rings. The Donut Hole in La Puente, a drive-through you enter and leave through the holes of two giant donuts, is described as a distant cousin of the rooftop kind.

One critic called the giant donuts part of a Los Angeles that "bordered on pop art, celebrating the effusiveness of life in the years after World War II" — the same city that gave America an orange juice stand shaped like an orange.
text.today: Municipal construction codes now generally prohibit oversize object-shaped buildings, so the survivors cannot be replaced, only kept.

sections.text:
— **Long John** — the Midwest, Canada and Texas.
— **Bar** — the West Coast: maple bar, chocolate bar, filled bar.
— **Éclair** — the Mid-Atlantic and central Canada, where it is marketed that way even though an éclair is choux pastry with fondant and a Long John is yeast dough.
— **Finger doughnut**, and **cream stick** when filled — parts of the Midwest.
— **Maple creamstick**, **maple bismarck**, **maple-glazed Long John** — the same pastry again, named by its icing.

**Bismarck** for a filled round holds in the Upper Midwest, where a case label will say it and nothing else; elsewhere it is a jelly donut. **Fry cake** for a cake donut survives on older signs. **Jimmies** for chocolate sprinkles belongs to Boston, Philadelphia and New England and is first recorded in 1930. **Bear claw** is Western American English, first attested in a Sacramento bakery advertisement on 13 March 1914. **Kolache** in Texas usually means a klobasnek, which Czech Texans will tell you is a different thing.

text.what: Two doughs, one kettle, and an argument every shop settles twice a day. Raised dough is lifted by yeast and takes about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C; cake batter is lifted by baking powder or soda and takes about 90 seconds at 190 to 198 °C. Yeast rings average 38 grams, cake rings 24 to 28. The fat numbers are where the published accounts stop agreeing, and this page lays both out rather than picking one.

sections.text:
Yeast and cake donuts share most of their ingredients. What separates them is the flour and the lift. Cake donuts use cake flour, around 7 to 8 percent protein, which crumbs rather than pulls, and they rise on baking powder or baking soda. Raised donuts use a stronger dough and baker's yeast, and they need time.

That difference sets everything downstream: how long the dough occupies the shop, how the ring is formed, how long it sits in the fat, how much fat it takes up, how big it comes out, and how long it is worth selling.

Yeast-raised rings fry about 150 seconds at 182 to 190 °C and average 38 grams. Cake rings fry about 90 seconds at 190 to 198 °C, turning once, and weigh 24 to 28 grams.

On oil, the published accounts diverge. One says yeast-raised donuts contain about 25 percent oil by weight and cake donuts around 20 percent, with extra fat mixed into the batter before frying. Another says cake runs 20 to 25 percent and yeast 25 to 35, and that commercial cake rings fry for 30 to 45 seconds at 191 °C.

Neither cites a laboratory. Both agree on the direction — the raised ring spends longer in the fat and carries more of it out — and disagree on the size of the gap. This project prints both.

When donut shops industrialised in the 1920s and 1930s, the raised dough was at a disadvantage: it needs time to rise and it is harder to handle. Baking soda was predictable and easy to automate, so most bakers went the cake route. The cake ring also appeared in American cookbooks a century earlier, in the 1830s, once pearlash was easy to buy.

The raised ring survived anyway, because a glazed raised donut is what most people mean by the word.

sections.h: What it means at the counter
sections.text:
*Inference —* a shop that runs both doughs well is running two processes with different clocks in one small kitchen, which is most of the work in a mom-and-pop donut shop and none of the work in a shop that buys its donuts in.

Which side of the case carries the flavours is a reading, not a count: cider, buttermilk, sour cream, blueberry and chocolate sit on the cake side, and the raised side holds glazed, bars, fritters and filled.

The Providence metropolitan area has been cited as having the most donut shops per capita in the United States: 25.3 shops per 100,000 people, as of 13 January 2010. Rhode Island is 48th by area among the states.

Canada has the highest concentration of donut shops per capita in the world and eats the most donuts per head; Japan is second by concentration. Over 4,600 Tim Hortons locations do most of that work.

sections.h: What this site can count, and what it cannot
sections.text:
This directory counts what OpenStreetMap records, on the date it was fetched, plus the shops written up here. That is a count of a map, not a census of a trade. Shops open and close faster than any map keeps up with, and a shop that nobody has added to OpenStreetMap is invisible to it.

The number to compare against — an actual national count of independent donut shops — does not exist in a form this project can cite. KQED's 2021 figure of more than 5,000 independent shops in California alone is the largest sourced number here, and it is one state.

/places/ draws every row on one map. /numbers/ counts them by state and by distance. Chains are marked as chains, because OpenStreetMap records a brand when a place has one, and can be taken off the map in a click.

sections.text:
Every record here is hand-written JSON, one file per node, and every field carries a provenance tier: cited (a named source), harvested (a tool fetched it from an open dataset), tradition (general knowledge of the trade, hedged in the prose), inference (this project reasoning from the above, and saying so), field (somebody stood there — nothing carries it yet).

The records are licensed CC BY 4.0.

The bulk of the cited material is Wikipedia, fetched as plain text on 16 September 2026 and listed article by article on the sources page, under CC BY-SA 4.0. Where a fact came from reporting instead — KQED on why California donut shops sell Chinese food, PBS Independent Lens on The Donut King — the record names the outlet, the writer and the date.

A fact this project could not source is either hedged in the prose and marked, or left out.

Place points come from OpenStreetMap contributors under ODbL 1.0, fetched state by state on the date the coverage page names, plus addresses geocoded through Nominatim. An absence in that data means the place was not in OpenStreetMap on the fetch date or has not been written up here. It is not a claim that a shop does not exist.
Pictures come from Wikimedia Commons, each with its licence, author and link beside it. Only CC0, public domain, CC BY, CC BY-SA and FAL are accepted.

Field observations. Menu prices with dates for most shops. Photographs for most records. Per-piece weights for shop donuts, which almost nobody publishes. Most towns. The coverage page keeps the current list.

text.what: What a donut shop sells besides donuts, region by region, and what this project can show evidence for. Egg rolls in Southern California, klobasniky in Texas, breakfast burritos in New Mexico, bacon egg and cheese in New York, biscuits and gravy in the South, boba almost anywhere after 2015.

sections.h: How a shop gets tagged here
sections.text:
A shop carries a counter tag when a source says so: its own menu, a photograph of the board, or a press piece that names the item. The tag says which. A shop with no counter tag has not been read, which is a fact about this project and not about the shop.

The national map is coarser, and says which kind of evidence it is using. OpenStreetMap rows are tagged from what the map itself records — the shop's name and its cuisine tags — so a place called "Donut & Burrito" lands on the burrito layer because it says so on the sign.

— **Southern California and the Central Valley**: egg rolls, chow mein, fried rice, croissant sandwiches. Cambodian-American and Chinese-American ownership, a hot case beside the donut case.
— **Texas**: kolaches and klobasniky, from gas stations to dedicated shops, statewide and well past the Czech counties.
— **New Mexico, Arizona, west Texas**: breakfast burritos, foil-wrapped, chile by name.
— **New York and New Jersey**: bacon egg and cheese on a kaiser roll, mostly at delis and bodegas rather than donut shops.
— **The South**: biscuits and gravy, and fried chicken in shops that lean that way.
— **Hawaii**: malasadas as the main event, with the rest of the case around them.
— **Everywhere, lately**: boba, and Korean corn dogs beside mochi donuts.

It is not fusion and it is not a gimmick. It is a second sale to the same customer at the same hour, in a business whose own product stops selling by mid-morning. The shop owners say this plainly when anyone asks them.

text.what: How one man's shop in La Habra became a trade for a community, and what happened to the man. Ted Ngoy fled the Khmer Rouge in 1975, trained at a chain, bought a shop in 1977, and by the mid-1980s had leased shops to more than a hundred sponsored families. He also gambled it away.

sections.text:
Ngoy was born in 1941 in Sisophon, near the Thai border, to a Chinese immigrant family; his mother, from Shantou, did not speak Khmer, which made getting by hard. Sent to Phnom Penh to study in 1967, he married Suganthini Khoeun, worked as a travel agent and a tour guide, and joined the military in 1970. Through his brother-in-law Sak Sutsakhan — chief of police and briefly president of Cambodia — he was made a major and military attaché in Thailand.

In 1975 he fled with his wife and three children and came through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program to Camp Pendleton.

He took a janitor's job at Peace Lutheran Church in Tustin and a second job at a gas station. He noticed how busy a local donut shop was and asked to learn. An affirmative-action hiring programme at Winchell's trained him, and he managed a store in Newport Beach, employing his wife and nephew.

In 1977 he bought Christy's Donuts in La Habra. It had not done well before. It did under the Ngoys, and they named every shop they bought after it. By 1979 there were more than 25.

The part that mattered was not the shops but the leasing. Ngoy trained relatives and refugees and leased shops to them. "I sponsored more than 100 families", he said, and claimed each as kin on official documents. He lived out of a motor home to open new locations up and down California. By 1987 there were 32 Christy's; at the peak he reckoned 65.

A family arrived, learned a trade in weeks, took a shop, and a few years later handed one to the next family. That is how a refugee community came to hold a large share of an American trade.

In 1977 the Ngoys went to Las Vegas and he saw Elvis. He also found the blackjack tables. He went back monthly for the shows and stayed for the cards, forged his wife's signature on cheques, borrowed from relatives who leased shops from him, and signed shops over when he could not repay. Refugees who had once come to him for help began to avoid him. Gamblers Anonymous did not take: "I cry, everybody cry. After cry, go back gambling."

The shops. In 1985 he and his wife became citizens as Ted and Christy; the pink box is attributed to him and to Ning Yen, who were setting other families up in the trade. KQED reported in 2021 that roughly 90 percent of California's 5,000-plus independent donut shops were Cambodian-owned.

Alice Gu's documentary The Donut King (2020) put the story in front of a national audience. Most people who recognise the pink box do not know either name.

text.what: Between 1940 and 1968 a Salt Lake City potato-flour company put more than three hundred shops on American streets. The company is gone. Some of the shops are not.

sections.h: A dry mix is a business model
sections.text: Al and Bob Pelton ate potato doughnuts in Germany and worked their way from wheat dough flavoured with potato water, through mashed potato, to a dry potato mix. The mix is the invention: it made the recipe shippable, and a shippable recipe can be franchised. They coined the word spudnut and opened in 1940.

Franchising began in 1946. In 1948 a new franchisee paid $50 plus the cost of a hundred sacks of spudnut flour. By 1952 a franchise cost $1,750 plus equipment, about $5,000 all in — roughly $109,550 in 2024 dollars — and the Peltons were on the cover of Mechanix Illustrated under the headline "Their Potatoes Make Dough".

Over 200 shops by 1948. More than 225 in 31 states by mid-1949. More than 300 in 38 states by 1954. 315 by 1968. The advertising ran "Coast to coast… Alaska to Mexico", with a cartoon Mr. Spudnut in parades.

The parent company no longer exists. Independent shops still trade under the name.

*Inference —* that is the most common shape of survival in this trade. Daylight Donuts, the Tulsa mix company founded in 1954, still supplies roughly 950 independently owned shops; if it went tomorrow the signs would stay up and the shops would keep frying. The infrastructure of American donuts is mostly flour suppliers and second-hand equipment, and both outlive their companies.

sections.text:
**39 cents each, 1 June 1968, North Kingstown, Rhode Island.** Frederick Alvin "Allie" Briggs opened Allie's Hand-Cut Do-nut Shop with about forty dollars in hand and a seven-thousand-dollar debt, and took $38 on the first day selling close to a hundred dozen.

**$50 plus a hundred sacks of flour, 1948.** What a new Spudnut Shops franchisee paid to open. By 1952 a franchise cost $1,750 plus equipment — an initial investment of about $5,000, or roughly $109,550 in 2024 dollars.

**2,400 calories and 144 grams of fat in a dozen, from 2004 onward.** Not a price, but the only per-dozen figure in this directory that somebody published — the Krispy Kreme Challenge prints it on the rules.

Menu prices with dates, for the shops written up here. A donut price changes faster than a record does, and an undated price on a directory page is worse than no price: a reader plans around it.

This project prints a price only with the date it was read and the source it came from. That leaves the page thin, and thin is the accurate state of it.

Not answered here. A national average would need dated menu reads across the country, which this project has not done. *Inference —* the spread is wide: a strip-mall dozen and a made-to-order dozen at a shop like Pip's are not the same product and are not priced as if they were.

text.what: Donut shop signs are older than the businesses behind them, which makes them unreliable evidence and excellent evidence at the same time.

sections.text:
Donut Wheel in Livermore was started in 1962 by Jack and Jean Weil, and got its name because a colleague heard Weil as "wheel". They sold in 1972. It has changed hands several times since and kept the name.

Randy's Donuts was a Big Donut Drive-In until 1976, when Robert Eskow bought it and named it after his son. Eskow sold it in 1978 to Ron and Larry Weintraub, who kept it. It was sold again in 2015. There has been no Randy behind the counter for most of the sign's life.

Christy's Donuts was named after Christy Ngoy. Shops trading as Christy's exist in Southern California today; this project has not established which, if any, descend from those shops.

sections.h: Franchises that left their signs behind
sections.text:
Spudnut Shops numbered more than 300 in 38 states by 1954 and 315 by 1968; the parent company no longer exists, and independent shops still trade under the name. A Spudnut sign today marks a shop that outlived a system.

Winchell's went from 293 shops in 1999 to about 100 in six states by 2025. The chain shrank; the independents its training seeded multiplied.

sections.h: What this means for reading a map
sections.text: *Inference —* the name on a donut shop is closer to a place name than a brand: it tells you what the corner has been called, not who is inside. A directory that treats the sign as the owner will be wrong on both counts, so this project records ownership only where a source names it.

sections.h: Why the sign is no help
sections.text:
Every Daylight Donuts store is independently owned and operated, and there are roughly 950 of them in 13 countries. The company in Tulsa sells mix — it started in 1954 as a flour company, with Tommy and Lucille Day making donut mix in the mornings and selling it out of the trunk of their car in the afternoons.

Spudnut Shops worked the same way from 1940 with a dry potato mix: more than 300 shops in 38 states by 1954, 315 by 1968, and then the parent company disappeared. Shops still trading under the name are not a chain; they are what a chain left behind.

A shop can look independent and not be. Top Pot makes donuts at two Seattle-area kitchens and trucks them to seventeen cafés, and supplies recipes to more than 7,000 Starbucks stores. Blue Star manufactures in one Portland facility and distributes to its shops rather than putting a fryer in each one.

Neither is doing anything wrong. But a reader looking for a family frying at two in the morning should be told the difference.

A shop counts as independent here when no company owns it, whatever the sign says. Where this project knows that a shop is owned by the family working in it, the record says so and names the source. Where it does not know, the record says nothing — which is where most shops in this directory currently stand.

The national map carries chain-owned locations too, marked as chains, because leaving them out would misrepresent what is on the ground and because OpenStreetMap records them by brand. Filtering them off is one click; pretending they are not there would be a different kind of map.

text.what: A donut shop that also sells egg rolls, or breakfast burritos, or bacon egg and cheese, or kolaches, is not being eccentric. It is doing arithmetic out loud. The people running those shops have said so in print, repeatedly, and this page collects what they said.

sections.h: The answer, from the people doing it
sections.text:
Jolly Chan opened China Express and Donut by the 24th Street BART station in San Francisco in 1993. He had come from Cambodia in 1981. Asked by KQED in 2021 why the two menus sit together, he said the combination "came out of necessity" — "We have to sell more stuff to make up the rent and the expense." His customer base, he said, was 80 percent Latino.

That is the whole mechanism. A donut shop's trade is over by ten in the morning. The rent is not.

Ted Ngoy, a Cambodian refugee who reached Camp Pendleton in 1975, trained at Winchell's, bought Christy's Donuts in La Habra in 1977, and then leased shops to relatives and to refugee families he sponsored — more than a hundred, by his own account. KQED reported that roughly 90 percent of California's 5,000-plus independent donut shops were Cambodian-owned.

A trade that arrives through one community carries that community's other food with it, and a fryer that is already hot does not care what goes in it.

The pattern repeats wherever an early-morning counter needs a second product:

— Southern California: egg rolls, chow mein and fried rice in a warmer beside the case.
— Texas: kolaches, and above all klobasniky — sausage in kolache dough — which means the shop runs an oven as well as a kettle.
— New Mexico and the Southwest: breakfast burritos, wrapped in foil, red or green.
— New York: the bacon, egg and cheese on a kaiser roll, at a deli or bodega where the donuts are bought in.
— The South: biscuits and gravy.
— The 2020s: boba, and Korean corn dogs beside mochi donuts.

*Inference —* the second menu is the most reliable sign that a shop is owned by the people working in it. A company-owned store sells what the company prints.

The combination gets written up as a quirk — as a joke about America, or a listicle item. The shops are describing a cost structure. Dorothy Chow, whose father built B & H Bakery Distributors after surviving the Cambodian genocide, told KQED he started it "to help our own people": the supply chain behind these shops was built by the same community that runs them.

This project tags what a shop sells beside its donuts, names where the tag came from, and leaves the quirk to somebody else.
